title: The Initiative
subtitle: Keep the move, or exchange it for a lasting advantage

steps.title: The first move is an initial advantage

narration.say: Both sides begin with the same material and the same arrangement of pieces. White has the first move.
Capablanca describes this initial opportunity to act first as the initiative. Other things being equal, it is an advantage.
Develop your pieces as quickly as possible, but do not treat development as a task disconnected from your opponent.
Capablanca asks White to hinder the opponent’s development by applying pressure wherever possible. Development and pressure should support each other.
First seek control of the centre. It helps your pieces act and makes it easier to keep the opponent responding.
If central control is unavailable, seek another positional advantage that allows you to maintain pressure.

steps.title: Do not surrender the initiative for nothing

narration.say: Keep the initiative as long as possible. Give it up only when you obtain something in exchange: a material or positional advantage.
A material gain must leave you able to withstand the opponent’s counterplay. Winning material is not enough if the resulting position cannot be defended.

steps.title: Survive the counterplay and act again

narration.say: After a favourable material gain, the opponent may temporarily take over the initiative.
Capablanca’s plan is to withstand that pressure and then use the extra material to resume active play. The exchange of advantages must be judged over the whole sequence.
Once the pieces are developed, Capablanca distinguishes three possible directions.
You may attack the king directly; improve a position that is already favourable; or gain material while temporarily conceding the initiative.
